prompt: Write an essay titled “To code well, avoid blunders”. It argues that writing good code is mostly a matter of avoiding catastrophic mistakes, not of having brilliant insights. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
Most programmers imagine that excellent software comes from flashes of genius: an elegant abstraction that unlocks a hard problem, a clever algorithm that outruns its rivals, a design so insightful that it seems to have always existed. We celebrate these moments, and we write about them in retrospectives and conference talks. But when I look at the codebases that have served people reliably for years, and at the wreckage of the ones that collapsed, I see something less glamorous. Good code is mostly the absence of catastrophic mistakes. The brilliant insight is a bonus. Avoiding the blunder is the job.

Consider what a catastrophic mistake looks like. It is rarely a subtle bug in a complicated function. It is a deleted production database because a script ran against the wrong environment. It is a password stored in plain text and then leaked in a log file. It is an integer overflow that silently turns a bank balance negative, or a date library that assumes every year has 365 days. These errors share a pattern: they are simple, they are easy to make, and they are expensive. A single one can erase months of careful work. The programmer who avoids them has not necessarily outthought anyone. They have simply refused to make the cheap, predictable errors that most software suffers from.

This reframing matters because it changes where effort should go. If good code were about insight, we would spend our time searching for the next clever idea. If good code is about avoiding blunders, we spend our time on dull, disciplined habits: validating inputs, checking return values, handling the error path instead of assuming the happy one, writing the test for the edge case nobody thought would happen, and reading our own diffs before submitting them. None of this is exciting. All of it prevents disasters.

Consider error handling. Many programs are written as though every network call succeeds, every file exists, and every user enters well-formed data. The code works beautifully in the demo and fails in the field. The blunder here is not ignorance of some advanced technique. It is the unexamined assumption. A developer who asks, at each external interaction, "What happens if this fails, and what will the user or the system see?" has eliminated a whole category of disasters. That question is simple, and asking it consistently is most of what separates robust software from fragile software.

Or consider the problem of shared state. Concurrency bugs have a reputation as mind-bending puzzles, and some certainly are. But many come from a plain mistake: two parts of a program reading and writing the same value without coordination, on the assumption that they will never overlap. The fix is rarely a brilliant new synchronization scheme. It is more often the discipline of minimizing shared mutable state to begin with, and of being suspicious whenever two things touch the same data. Avoiding the blunder beats cleverly resolving it after the fact.

There is an objection worth taking seriously. Someone might argue that this philosophy produces timid code: code that is defensive, bloated with checks, and afraid of its own shadow. That is a fair worry, but it misreads the goal. Avoiding blunders does not mean adding every conceivable guard. It means being deliberate about the failures that matter. A check on user input at the system boundary is essential; the same check repeated fifteen times inside trusted internal functions is noise. Good engineers distinguish between the risks that could ruin the system and the ones that cost nothing to ignore. The skill is judgment about which blunders are catastrophic, and that judgment is itself a form of discipline.

The strongest evidence for this view is in how experienced teams actually work. They rely on code review, not because reviewers are geniuses, but because a second pair of eyes catches the obvious mistake the author was too close to see. They use linters, type checkers, and continuous integration, not because these tools are intelligent, but because they never get tired of checking for the same common errors. They write runbooks and perform rollbacks rehearsals, anticipating the operational slip that will eventually happen. None of these practices promise brilliance. All of them reduce the chance of the mistake that brings everything down.

I suspect the reason we overvalue insight is that blunders are invisible when they don't happen. Nobody writes an essay about the outage that never occurred or the data breach that a validation check quietly prevented. Success in this area is measured by absence, and absence is hard to celebrate. But it is the honest measure. The programmer who ships code for ten years without a major incident has probably done something more valuable than the one who produced a dazzling design and a fragile system.

So if you want to write good code, start by asking what could go catastrophically wrong, and make that unlikely. Check the things you assumed. Read your changes as if someone else wrote them. Test the path where things fail. The insights will come, sometimes, and they are worth having. But they will not save you if the basics are broken. Avoiding blunders is not the glamorous part of programming. It is the part that keeps working.
